title.en: Word types II: the unchangeable words

summary.en: Adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, particles and interjections, plus a method to identify any word.
summary.bs: Prilozi, prijedlozi, veznici, rječce i uzvici, i metod da prepoznaš bilo koju riječ.

en.one: A prilog (adverb) tells how, when, where or how much something happens. It never changes form.
en.explain: How to spot it: it answers kako? (how? – brzo, dobro, lijepo), kada? (when? – danas, sutra, sada), gdje? (where? – ovdje, tamo, gore) or koliko? (how much? – mnogo, malo, vrlo). Many adverbs look like the neuter adjective ending in -o: brz → brzo, dobar → dobro.
en.example: 'Danas sam brzo završila posao i sada sam ovdje.' Adverbs: danas, brzo, sada, ovdje.
en.why: Adverbs make sentences precise without adding new endings to learn.
en.mixup: 'dobro' can be an adverb ('Radi dobro' – he works well) or the neuter adjective ('dobro dijete' – a good child). Check what it describes.

en.one: A prijedlog (preposition) stands before a noun or pronoun and shows place, time, cause or relation: u, na, s(a), bez, od, do, za, prema.
en.explain: How to spot it: it never changes, and the word after it is always in a specific case. That's the key rule: the preposition chooses the case. 'bez' always takes the genitive (bez šećera), 's/sa' meaning 'with' takes the instrumental (s prijateljem), 'u' and 'na' take the accusative for direction and the locative for location.
en.example: 'Idem na posao sa sestrom.' na + accusative (posao), sa + instrumental (sestrom).
en.why: Prepositions are the main way you meet cases in daily speech.
en.mixup: 's' becomes 'sa' before words starting with s, z, š, ž or for clarity: sa sestrom, sa mnom.

en.one: A veznik (conjunction) links words or clauses: i, a, ali, ili, jer, da, kad, ako, iako.
en.explain: Coordinating: i (and), a (and/while – a mild contrast), ali (but), ili (or), pa (so/and then). Subordinating: jer (because), da (that / to), kad (when), ako (if), iako (although), dok (while). 'a' has no English twin: 'Ja pijem čaj, a on kafu (kavu)' – I drink tea, and (while) he drinks coffee.
en.example: 'Ostala sam kod kuće jer sam bila bolesna, ali sutra dolazim.'
en.why: Conjunctions turn short sentences into real explanations: reasons, conditions and contrasts.
en.mixup: 'i' joins similar things; 'a' contrasts two different ones. 'Ja sam iz Tuzle, a ona je iz Splita' sounds more natural than with 'i'.

en.one: A rječca (Croatian: čestica) is a small word that adds meaning or tone: li, ne, zar, da, baš, čak, samo, još.
en.explain: The most important ones: 'ne' (not) for negation, 'li' for questions (Dolaziš li?), 'da' and 'ne' as yes and no, 'zar' for surprised questions (Zar ne znaš? – You really don't know?), 'baš' (really, exactly), 'čak' (even).
en.example: 'Je li to baš tvoje auto?' 'Zar si već stigao?'
en.why: Particles carry the tone of a conversation. Recognising them helps you hear surprise, doubt and emphasis.
en.mixup: Bosnian school grammar says rječca, Croatian says čestica. Same idea, different name.

en.one: An uzvik (interjection) expresses a feeling or a sound: joj, uh, au, eh, hej, bravo, ajme.
en.explain: Interjections stand outside the sentence's grammar, often at the start, followed by a comma or exclamation mark. Some are very regional: 'joj' and 'ajme' (oh no / wow) are everywhere in Bosnia and Croatia.
en.example: 'Joj, zaboravio sam ključeve!' 'Bravo, uspjela si!' 'Hej, kako si?'
en.why: They make your speech sound native and help you catch the emotion behind a sentence.
en.mixup: Onomatopoeic words (sounds) also count: 'Pas laje: av-av.' 'Mačka: mjau.'

en.one: A four-question method to identify any word.
en.explain: 1. Can you ask ko? (tko?) / šta? (što?) and does it have a gender? → imenica. 2. Does it show a person (-m, -š, -mo) or end in -ti/-ći in the dictionary? → glagol. 3. Does it answer kakav?/koji?/čiji? and agree with a noun? → pridjev. 4. Does it never change? → prilog (kako/kada/gdje), prijedlog (before a noun), veznik (links clauses), rječca or uzvik.
en.example: 'Sutra moja mlađa sestra putuje vozom (vlakom) u Zagreb.' sutra = prilog, moja = zamjenica, mlađa = pridjev, sestra = imenica, putuje = glagol, vozom (vlakom) = imenica, u = prijedlog, Zagreb = imenica.
en.why: Once you can label words, the case and agreement rules become easy to apply.
en.mixup: Endings change, so look at the word's job, not only its form: 'dobro' can be prilog or pridjev.

explain.en: It stands before a noun and puts it in the genitive.
'zar' adds surprise or disbelief to a question.
It describes HOW she sings, so it's an adverb.
